title: The Proof That Never Arrives
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer uses a letter the Fire Fellows sent to Spokane's wildfire survivors, drawn from 18 months of Los Angeles fire recovery, to argue that community preparedness is systematically undervalued because prevention never produces visible proof of the disaster it averted. She reports that after six waves of survivor surveys, most Los Angeles fire victims remain displaced with worsening mental health and near-zero government assistance, while community and faith organizations are the only institutions rated positively. She argues this proves durable civic infrastructure is built in ordinary times, not crises, and closes with a personal leadership challenge: know your neighbors now, because grief is a poor teacher of new habits.
points: Schafer's central mechanism for civic neglect: 'prevention never produces evidence of itself,' so leaders keep treating readiness as optional because no report ever proves the catastrophe that didn't happen.

The Los Angeles data she cites is stark: three-quarters of Palisades and two-thirds of Altadena residents remain displaced 18 months out, and government satisfaction sits under 20% versus 51% for community organizations.
Her practical leadership move is naming a true, uncomfortable recovery timeline up front, which she argues is 'the kindest thing a community can do in its first week' precisely because it is free.

She reframes neighborliness as free, permission-less civic infrastructure, the one resource still standing at month eighteen after formal government and insurance systems exhausted what they knew how to do.
quotes: The reason we do not prepare is not cost, because the cost of not acting on the truth is far higher, in money and in people. I think the reason is that prevention never produces evidence of itself.
Three-quarters of Palisades residents and two-thirds of Altadena residents are still displaced. Eighty-five percent of the people who lost everything are still in temporary housing.

Satisfaction with the federal, state, and local governments' response all sat below twenty percent. Satisfaction with community-based organizations sat at fifty-one, the only institution in the entire study with more support than opposition.
Nobody built those congregations after the fire. They were already there: decades of Sunday mornings and gatherings and shared meals, none of it undertaken as preparedness.
It means the most durable civic infrastructure we have costs almost nothing and requires no one's permission.
Naming the true time for a recovery arc honestly may be the kindest thing a community can do in its first week. It is also free.
